title: Cold Flow Fundamentals
scopeHtml: Scope: what Flow is, cold semantics, builders, terminal operators, Flow vs Sequence vs suspend List, context preservation, exception transparency, Flow/FlowCollector/SafeCollector internals, Room/DataStore sources.

questions.promptHtml: What is a Kotlin Flow, and how is it different from a suspend fun that returns a List?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand Flow as "an asynchronous stream of 0..N values over time" rather than "LiveData with operators".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Flow is a cold, asynchronous stream: it can emit many values over time, and each emission can suspend. Nothing runs until someone calls a terminal operator like collect. A suspend fun returning List gives me one value, all at once, after everything has finished. With Flow the consumer can process item 1 while the producer is still working on item 2, and the stream can be unbounded.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Think in the 2x2 of "how many values" and "sync vs async":

One value Many values
Sync T Sequence<T> / Iterable<T>
Async (suspending) suspend fun(): T Flow<T>

Flow is the bottom-right cell. Mechanically, Flow<T> is an interface with exactly one method: suspend fun collect(collector: FlowCollector<T>). A producer pushes values into collector.emit(value), which is itself a suspend function. So the producer is suspended until the consumer's lambda returns for that value. There is no queue between them by default, which is why a Flow is sequential and gives natural back-pressure.

Key properties:

  • Cold: no work happens at declaration. val f = flow { ... } only builds an object.
  • Sequential by default: the producer and the collector run in the same coroutine, one value at a time.
  • Cancellable: cancelling the collecting coroutine cancels the producer, because the producer literally runs inside collect.
  • Structured: it runs in the collector's coroutine context (context preservation, see Q494).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun loadAll(): List<Int> {          // caller sees nothing until all 3 are done (~300ms)
    val out = mutableListOf<Int>()
    repeat(3) { delay(100); out += it }
    return out
}

fun stream(): Flow<Int> = flow {            // caller sees 0 at 100ms, 1 at 200ms, 2 at 300ms
    repeat(3) { delay(100); emit(it) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "Flow is like LiveData". LiveData is hot, lifecycle-aware, holds one value. Cold Flow has none of those.
  • Believing val f = flow { println("run") } prints something. It does not.
  • Thinking Flow is multi-threaded by default. It is not; it runs in the collector's context.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Flow a replacement for RxJava Observable? → Closest to a cold Observable with back-pressure built in via suspension; no Single/Maybe/Completable split, those become suspend functions.
  2. Can a Flow be infinite? → Yes (while (true) { emit(..); delay(..) }), consumed with take, first, or cancellation.
  3. Why is emit suspending? → So the producer is paused while the collector processes the value; this is the back-pressure mechanism and also lets the collector be a suspend lambda.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "stream of values, collect it". Senior: "interface with one suspend method, producer runs inside the collector's coroutine, so cancellation, context and exceptions all flow naturally with no extra machinery; back-pressure is just suspension."

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that treat Flow as "async List" load whole tables and then wrap in a Flow, losing the progressive-rendering benefit and the memory benefit.

questions.promptHtml: What are the ways to create a Flow (flow {}, flowOf, asFlow, emptyFlow), and when do you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic fluency; also the follow-up about asFlow on a Sequence/lambda reveals depth.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: flow { emit(x) } is the general builder for anything that needs suspend calls or loops. flowOf(a, b, c) is a fixed set of values, good for tests and defaults. asFlow() converts an existing collection, range, sequence, or a suspend () -> T lambda. emptyFlow() is a flow with no values. For callback APIs I use callbackFlow, which is a different chunk's topic.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• flow { }: the lambda has receiver FlowCollector<T>, so emit is available. It creates a SafeFlow (subclass of AbstractFlow). The lambda runs fresh on each collect.
  • flowOf(vararg): emits the given values then completes. flowOf(x) for a single value.
  • asFlow(): extension on Iterable, Sequence, Array, IntRange/LongRange, Iterator, and on function types () -> T and suspend () -> T (the latter gives a one-element flow that runs the call per collection, handy for "wrap this suspend call as a flow").
  • emptyFlow(): completes immediately, no values.
  • channelFlow { } / callbackFlow { }: for concurrent emission or callback bridging; they buffer through a channel. Out of scope here.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val a = flow { emit(1); delay(10); emit(2) }
val b = flowOf("x", "y")
val c = listOf(1, 2, 3).asFlow()
val d = (1..5).asFlow()
val e = ::fetchUser.asFlow()            // suspend () -> T lambda form: only works for () -> T references
val f = emptyFlow<Int>()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• flowOf(list) gives Flow<List<T>> with ONE emission; list.asFlow() gives one emission per element.
  • Using flow {} and calling emit from inside launch in it (Q511).
  • sequence.asFlow() does not make the sequence async; blocking sequence code still blocks the collector's thread.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. flowOf(listOf(1,2)) vs listOf(1,2).asFlow()? → One emission of the list vs two emissions of ints.
  2. Is a flow created by flowOf cold? → Yes in semantics; each collector gets the values again, though the values themselves are already computed.
  3. How do you wrap a one-shot suspend call as a Flow? → flow { emit(api.get()) }; it re-runs the call per collector.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists builders. Senior notes flowOf(list) vs asFlow(), that all of them re-run per collector, and picks flow {} when emission needs suspend work.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flowOf(cachedList) default in a repository made UI tests pass while the real path (Room) emitted per-row updates; the mismatch hid a bug until QA.

questions.promptHtml: What are terminal operators in Flow? Name the common ones and say what each does and what it throws on an empty flow.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Terminal operators are where Flow actually starts; empty-flow behavior is a classic production crash.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Terminal operators are suspend functions that start collection and produce a result or just consume. collect runs a lambda per value, toList/toSet gather everything, first() takes the first value and cancels the upstream, single() requires exactly one, fold/reduce aggregate, count counts, and launchIn(scope) collects in a new coroutine and returns a Job. first() and single() throw NoSuchElementException on an empty flow; use firstOrNull() / singleOrNull() to avoid that.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Operator Result Empty flow Notes
collect { } Unit completes suspends until flow completes
toList()/toSet() collection empty never returns on infinite flow; memory grows
first() T NoSuchElementException cancels upstream after first value
first { pred } T NoSuchElementException if none match
firstOrNull() T? null
single() T NoSuchElementException; IllegalArgumentException("Flow has more than one element") if 2+ must see completion to know
singleOrNull() T? null returns null if 2+ elements
fold(init) { acc, v -> } R init
reduce { acc, v -> } T NoSuchElementException no initial value
count() Int 0
launchIn(scope) Job non-suspending; use with onEach

first() implements early exit by throwing an internal AbortFlowException through the producer to unwind it, then catching it in the operator. That means your finally blocks in the producer do run, and a try/catch(Exception) swallowing it in the producer is a bug.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val latest = repo.prices().first()                  // one-shot read from a stream
val maybe  = repo.prices().firstOrNull()
repo.events().onEach { render(it) }.launchIn(viewModelScope)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• single() on a Room flow: Room emits again on writes; single() waits for completion, which never comes, so it hangs.
  • Calling toList() on an endless flow (hangs, OOM).
  • launchIn with collect afterwards; launchIn is itself the terminal operator.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. launchIn(scope) vs scope.launch { flow.collect {} }? → Equivalent; launchIn is sugar that returns the Job.
  2. Why does first() not leak the producer? → It cancels via AbortFlowException, so the producer is unwound and finally runs.
  3. Why does reduce throw on empty but fold does not? → reduce has no seed to return.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists names. Senior knows empty/many behavior, first() cancellation mechanism, and the danger of toList()/single() on non-terminating (Room, DataStore) flows.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash NoSuchElementException: Expected at least one element on first launch traced to prefs.data.map{..}.first() over an empty source after a filter.

questions.promptHtml: What does "cold" mean for a Flow? If two collectors collect the same flow {}, what happens, and how is this different from a hot stream?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The #1 conceptual question on Flow; the follow-up decides whether you know shareIn/stateIn exist for a reason.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Cold means the producer block is a recipe, not a running process. Every call to collect executes the flow {} lambda from the start, independently, in the collector's coroutine. Two collectors means two executions, two network calls, two independent sequences of values. A hot stream like SharedFlow/StateFlow exists independently of collectors, and collectors just observe values emitted by someone else. To share one execution among collectors, I convert with shareIn or stateIn.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
cold:   collectorA.collect --> runs flow{} copy #1 --> value stream #1
        collectorB.collect --> runs flow{} copy #2 --> value stream #2

hot:    producer (one) --> SharedFlow --> collectorA
                                     \-> collectorB   (both see the same emissions)

Consequences:

  • Side effects in the builder (network, DB, log, counters) happen per collector.
  • Late collectors of a cold flow still get everything from the start; late collectors of a hot flow miss earlier values (unless replay).
  • No collectors means no work and no resource use; hot streams may keep running with zero collectors (unless SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed).
  • Cancelling a collector cancels only its own run.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val f = flow {
    println("start")
    emit(fetchPrice())
}
launch { f.collect { } }   // prints start, 1 network call
launch { f.collect { } }   // prints start again, 2nd network call
// Share one run:
val shared = f.shareIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), replay = 1)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Exposing a flow { api.call() } from a repository to several UI collectors and assuming one call.
  • Believing stateIn/shareIn makes the upstream hot forever; with WhileSubscribed it is restarted when subscribers go to zero (after the timeout).
  • Assuming "cold" means "slow" or "lazy evaluation of each element". It is about the whole pipeline start.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Room Flow cold? → Yes; each collector registers its own invalidation observer and runs its own query.
  2. Is StateFlow ever cold? → No, it always has a value and exists independent of collectors.
  3. What does shareIn(WhileSubscribed(5000)) do on rotation? → Upstream stays alive for 5 s with zero subscribers, so config change does not restart it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "cold = starts on collect". Senior: "each collector gets an independent execution, so side effects duplicate; I decide per flow whether to share, with what replay and stop timeout, and I know the cost of N collectors on a hot-path query."

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard screen with 4 collectors on the same repo flow fired 4 identical API calls on every open, quadrupling backend load for that endpoint (see Q500).

questions.promptHtml: When would you return Flow<T>, Sequence<T>, or suspend fun(): List<T>? Why can't you use a Sequence for async data?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests API design judgment and understanding of suspension vs blocking.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: suspend fun(): List<T> for a one-shot result that is bounded and small enough to hold in memory. Flow<T> for values arriving over time or when I want to start consuming before the producer is done, and when I need cancellation and suspension. Sequence<T> for synchronous lazy computation on in-memory or blocking data. A sequence block can only call suspend functions via SequenceScope's restricted suspension (@RestrictsSuspension), so I cannot delay or call a network suspend function in it; if I block inside a sequence I block the thread.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Sequence is lazy and pull-based: the consumer calls iterator.next() and blocks the thread until the next item is computed. sequence { yield(x) } uses suspension internally, but @RestrictsSuspension forbids arbitrary suspend calls.
  • Flow is push-based with suspension: the producer calls emit, which can suspend; the collector can be on any dispatcher and can suspend.
  • List is eager: all work done before the caller sees anything.
Need Pick
One result, bounded suspend fun(): List<T>
Progressive results / stream / observation Flow<T>
In-memory lazy pipeline (CPU only) Sequence<T>
Observe DB changes Flow<T>

Memory: list.map{}.filter{} creates intermediate lists; Sequence and Flow process element by element.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Wrong: blocks the collecting thread, cannot call suspend API
fun pages(): Sequence<Page> = sequence { while (true) yield(api.blockingGet()) } // blocking

// Right
fun pages(): Flow<Page> = flow { var n = 0; while (true) emit(api.get(n++)) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping a blocking Sequence in asFlow() and collecting on Main: still blocks Main.
  • Returning Flow<List<T>> from a one-shot call "for consistency", forcing callers to first().
  • Using Flow for a single value; a suspend fun is simpler and clearer.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not make every repository method return Flow? → Extra ceremony, cold re-execution surprises, and one-shot semantics are lost.
  2. How does Sequence.asFlow() behave? → Pulls the sequence in the collector's context, each next() blocks.
  3. Can a Flow be consumed by blocking code? → runBlocking { flow.toList() }, but it blocks a thread; avoid on Main.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior states the push vs pull difference, the @RestrictsSuspension reason, and the API-design rule "suspend for one, Flow for many or changing".

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A pagination helper built on sequence {} with blocking OkHttp calls ran on Dispatchers.Main through asFlow() and caused a 2.1% ANR rate until moved to flow {} plus flowOn(IO).

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between flow.collect { }, flow.onEach { }.launchIn(scope), and scope.launch { flow.collect { } }? What happens to code after collect?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: collect suspends until the flow completes; people write code after it and wonder why it never runs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: collect is a suspend call that returns only when the flow completes, so the code after it runs only for finite flows. launchIn and scope.launch { collect } are the same thing: they start a new coroutine that does the collection and return a Job immediately, so my current coroutine continues. For an endless flow (Room, StateFlow, DataStore) I must collect in its own coroutine if I need to do other things in the same scope.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
launchIn is defined as scope.launch { collect() }. onEach { } is an intermediate operator (it transforms the flow) and launchIn is the terminal operator that triggers it. Two flows collected sequentially in one coroutine means the second is never reached if the first is endless:

viewModelScope.launch {
    userFlow.collect { ... }      // never completes (Room/StateFlow)
    orderFlow.collect { ... }     // NEVER reached
}

Fix with two launches or launchIn:

userFlow.onEach { ... }.launchIn(viewModelScope)
orderFlow.onEach { ... }.launchIn(viewModelScope)

If both feed one UI state, use combine (see operators chunk). Exceptions: an uncaught exception in launchIn goes to the scope's handler like any launch; wrap with catch upstream.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val job = repo.items().onEach { adapter.submit(it) }.catch { log(it) }.launchIn(lifecycleScope)
job.cancel() // stops collection and upstream producer

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sequential collect on two endless flows.
  • launchIn(GlobalScope) leaking.
  • Forgetting that catch placed after onEach does catch exceptions in that onEach lambda, but one placed before it does not.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does launchIn return before values arrive? → Yes, it returns a Job immediately.
  2. How does lifecycle fit? → Use repeatOnLifecycle/flowWithLifecycle for UI (lifecycle chunk).
  3. What if the collector lambda throws? → Collection stops, the exception propagates through collect into the caller or the launch scope.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior notes the lambda placement rule for catch, the sequential-endless-flow trap, and that the Job handle is how cancellation is controlled.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "settings" screen never updated its second section because two Room flows were collected back-to-back in one launch.

questions.promptHtml: Explain Flow's context preservation property. Where does the producer code of flow { } run, and how do you change the dispatcher correctly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Knowing flowOn and why withContext inside flow {} throws is a staple senior question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A flow must emit in the same coroutine context it is collected in; that is "context preservation". So the flow {} lambda runs in whatever context the collector calls collect from. To move upstream work to another dispatcher I use flowOn(Dispatchers.IO), which affects only operators upstream of it. Using withContext around emit violates the invariant and throws IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
flow { A }  .map { B }  .flowOn(IO)  .map { C }  .collect { D }
|<----- runs on IO ------>|          |<-- collector's context -->|

flowOn introduces a boundary: upstream is collected in a separate coroutine with the new context, connected to downstream through a channel (buffer, default BUFFERED = 64 elements on JVM/Android, fused with buffer() calls). So flowOn also adds concurrency between the producer and collector, not just a dispatcher switch. Only the dispatcher/context elements are changed; the Job remains the child of the collector's job so cancellation is preserved.

Why the rule exists: combined with exception transparency, it keeps operator semantics predictable. If emit could be called from any thread/context, operators like map, catch or onCompletion could run in unknown contexts and break try/catch expectations.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun loadItems(): Flow<Item> = flow {
    emit(dao.slowQuery())     // blocking call, runs on IO due to flowOn below
}.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)

// Broken
flow { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(1) } }   // IllegalStateException on collect

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Placing flowOn after collect-side operators and expecting them to move.
  • Multiple flowOn: each applies to the segment above it up to the previous flowOn.
  • Assuming flowOn(Dispatchers.Main) is needed to update UI; the collector's context already decides that.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does flowOn change the collector's dispatcher? → No, only upstream.
  2. What does flowOn cost? → One extra coroutine plus a channel buffer; avoid when no switch needed.
  3. Is withContext safe around the whole collect? → Yes, it is the outer boundary; the violation is only for emitting from a different context than collection.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior explains that flowOn adds a channel and concurrency, and that a Main-safe repository uses flowOn(ioDispatcher) inside rather than forcing callers to choose.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Repository flows without flowOn ran Room-adjacent JSON parsing on Main, causing 40-60 ms jank spikes at list refresh.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate's PR adds disk caching to a repository. QA reports that opening the Feed crashes 100% of the time on debug builds and on release for 8% of users (those with a stale cache). Stack excerpt:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated:
    Flow was collected in [StandaloneCoroutine{Active}@3c1a, Dispatchers.Main.immediate],
    but emission happened in [DispatchedCoroutine{Active}@7d2, Dispatchers.IO].
    Please refer to 'flow' documentation or use 'flowOn' instead
    at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.internal.SafeCollector_commonKt.checkContext
    at com.app.FeedRepo$feed$1.invokeSuspend(FeedRepo.kt:31)

Code:

fun feed(): Flow<List<Post>> = flow {
    val cached = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { cache.read() }
    if (cached != null) emit(cached)
    withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        val fresh = api.fetchFeed()
        cache.write(fresh)
        emit(fresh)
    }
}

Only the second block emits inside withContext. 92% of users have a fresh cache and the API call is skipped by an early return elsewhere, which is why it was not caught. A red herring in the PR: the team also changed Moshi to codegen.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why it only crashes sometimes, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap the whole thing in withContext(Dispatchers.Main)" or "catch the IllegalStateException". Both hide the contract; the first moves network onto Main.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which dispatcher does the collector use (Main.immediate per the trace)? Is this only the debug check or also release? (SafeCollector check is always on, release too.) Is there other code that emits in this repo? Did the crash start with this PR? (Yes.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert or hotfix behind a flag; the hotfix is a 3-line change so I'd ship it rather than roll back, with the stale-cache path tested first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) emit inside withContext in different context: matches the message exactly. (b) Moshi codegen change: red herring, trace points at FeedRepo.kt:31 and checkContext. (c) Dispatcher mix-up in tests: no.
  4. How I'd verify each: Read trace line 31 (the emit(fresh) inside withContext), write a runTest that forces a stale cache and collects with toList(), which reproduces without a device.
  5. Root cause: withContext(IO) changes the coroutine context; emit then goes through SafeCollector, which compares the emitting context with the collector's. They differ, so it throws. It was intermittent because the second block only runs when the cache is stale or missing.
  6. Fix:
fun feed(): Flow<List<Post>> = flow {
    cache.read()?.let { emit(it) }       // suspend fun, internally main-safe
    val fresh = api.fetchFeed()
    cache.write(fresh)
    emit(fresh)
}.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)

Long term: make cache.read/write and api.fetchFeed main-safe suspend functions (they do their own withContext), so the flow body needs no dispatcher at all; keep flowOn only for blocking work in the flow body. 7. Prevention: a unit test per branch (cache hit, miss, stale) with a collector on a different test dispatcher; a code-review rule "no withContext around emit"; enable the lint check for flow + withContext if available in the team's detekt rules. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not catch IllegalStateException, because the flow's contract is already broken and the downstream state is unpredictable. I would not use channelFlow just to dodge the check; that is only warranted when I truly need concurrent emission.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the cache read must happen concurrently with the API call? → Use channelFlow { launch { send(cache.read()) }; send(api.fetch()) } or merge of two flows; send is thread-safe.
  • Would withContext(Dispatchers.Main.immediate) { emit(x) } be fine if the collector is on Main.immediate? → The check compares the context elements, ignoring the new coroutine's own Job, so identical dispatcher passes. It is allowed but pointless; I would still remove it, because it is one refactor away from a crash.
  • Why did tests pass? → Unit tests used Dispatchers.Unconfined / one test dispatcher, so context matched.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a team that wrapped Room-less file I/O in withContext inside flow{}; passing under UnconfinedTestDispatcher, crashing only on real devices when the cache expired weekly. Added a CI test using StandardTestDispatcher for collector and Dispatchers.IO for the repo.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests catching the exception or moving everything to Main.
  • Hire: identifies emit-in-different-context and fixes with flowOn.
  • Strong hire: also explains why it was intermittent, the SafeCollector check, main-safe suspend functions as the long-term pattern, and the test that reproduces it.

questions.promptHtml: What is exception transparency in Flow, and how does it affect where you put try/catch versus the catch operator?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Exposes whether you know catch only handles upstream exceptions and that swallowing downstream exceptions in a producer is illegal.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Exception transparency says a flow must not hide exceptions thrown by its downstream (the collector or later operators). If emit throws, the producer must let it propagate and stop emitting. Practically: the catch operator catches exceptions from upstream only, never from the collect lambda or operators below it. And I must not wrap emit() in a try/catch that swallows the exception, since that breaks the rule and the runtime throws IllegalStateException: Flow exception transparency is violated if I then emit again.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
flow { emit() } -> map -> catch{} -> onEach -> collect{}
|<--- catch sees these --->|     |<-- catch does NOT see these -->|

Because the producer runs inside collect and emit calls the downstream lambda directly, a downstream exception is thrown out of emit() inside the producer. If the producer catches it and continues, the collector sees the exception "vanish" and later values keep arriving even though collector code has failed. SafeCollector records that emit threw and, on the next emit, throws the transparency IllegalStateException.

Allowed patterns inside producers: catch exceptions from your own code (e.g. API call) before emit, or use catch with rethrow of what you do not handle.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: catches downstream failure too
flow {
    try { emit(api.get()) } catch (e: Exception) { emit(fallback) }  // if collector throws, we emit again -> ISE
}

// Correct
flow {
    val v = try { api.get() } catch (e: IOException) { fallback }
    emit(v)
}

flow.map { parse(it) }
    .catch { e -> emit(Error(e)) }       // sees upstream + map
    .collect { render(it) }               // exceptions here propagate to the caller

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping collect in try/catch for upstream errors: works but loses catch's ability to emit a fallback value.
  • catch { } swallowing CancellationException: in current versions catch does not catch cancellation of the collector, but your own try/catch(Exception) inside the producer will.
  • Putting catch before the throwing operator.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does catch catch exceptions from onEach above it? → Yes, anything upstream of it.
  2. How do you handle errors in the collect lambda? → try/catch around collect, or move the logic into onEach placed before catch.
  3. What does retry / retryWhen do about this? → They re-collect upstream on failure; only upstream exceptions, same rule.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior states the formal rule, shows the ISE message for violation, and puts the try/catch only around the risky call.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A producer-side try/catch(Exception) around emit swallowed a downstream JsonException and kept emitting, leading to an inconsistent UI list and a silent failure for 2 weeks.

questions.promptHtml: How is Flow implemented internally? Explain Flow, FlowCollector, AbstractFlow and SafeCollector, and why a library should not implement Flow directly.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who use Flow from those who can reason about its guarantees and debug stack traces.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Flow<T> is an interface with one method, suspend fun collect(collector: FlowCollector<T>). FlowCollector<T> is a fun interface with suspend fun emit(value: T). The flow {} builder creates a SafeFlow, a subclass of AbstractFlow, whose collect wraps my collector in a SafeCollector that enforces the two contracts at runtime: context preservation and exception transparency. Operators like map are just new Flows whose collect calls the upstream's collect with a wrapping collector. Third parties are discouraged from implementing Flow directly because they would have to uphold those invariants by hand; AbstractFlow or the builders do it for you.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
public interface Flow<out T> { public suspend fun collect(collector: FlowCollector<T>) }
public fun interface FlowCollector<in T> { public suspend fun emit(value: T) }

Chain: flow { emit(1) }.map { it * 2 }.collect { print(it) }

collect(lambda L)
 -> mapFlow.collect(L)
     -> upstreamSafeFlow.collect( C2 = { v -> L.emit(v*2) } )
         -> AbstractFlow.collect(C2): SafeCollector(C2, coroutineContext).let { block(it) }
             -> user block calls safeCollector.emit(1)
                  -> checkContext(); C2.emit(1) -> L.emit(2)

So an entire pipeline is a nested chain of calls on one stack; there are no intermediate queues unless buffer/flowOn/channelFlow is used. That is why Flow is cheap, why cancellation works, and why stack traces of Flow code are deep.

SafeCollector.emit:

  1. currentContext.ensureActive(): throws if cancelled (this is why emit is a cooperative cancellation point).
  2. Checks that currentContext equals the collector's context (ignoring the Job identity differences) and throws "Flow invariant is violated" otherwise. A fast path skips the full comparison when contexts are identical.
  3. If a previous emit threw, and you emit again, it throws the "exception transparency is violated" error.

Modern versions have Flow documented as "not stable for inheritance in 3rd party libraries", since kotlinx.coroutines may add members. unsafeFlow is the internal builder used by operators that guarantee the invariants by construction (not public API).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// A minimal custom operator written the way the library does it
fun <T, R> Flow<T>.myMap(f: suspend (T) -> R): Flow<R> = flow {
    collect { value -> emit(f(value)) }   // collects in the same context, emits in the same context
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Implementing Flow<T> as an object with a collect that switches dispatchers.
  • Assuming operators run on separate coroutines. They do not; only flowOn, buffer, conflate, produceIn, channelFlow-based operators (flatMapMerge, combine, merge, debounce...) introduce coroutines.
  • Treating SafeCollector as a public type; it is internal.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is emit a cancellation point? → SafeCollector calls ensureActive per emission, so a flow that emits regularly is cancellable; a tight loop with no emit is not (Q501).
  2. What is the cost of a long operator chain? → One extra emit call and a lambda object per operator per element; negligible versus I/O but visible in 1M-element CPU flows.
  3. How do onCompletion and catch work then? → They are flow {}-style wrappers with try/catch/finally around collect of the upstream.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows collect and emit. Senior can sketch the nested-collector call chain, name SafeCollector's three checks, and explain why there are no queues in a plain pipeline.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A deep StackOverflowError-looking trace in a 15-operator chain was misread as a bug; understanding the nested-call model made the real culprit (a blocking call in map on Main) obvious.

questions.promptHtml: How does a Room DAO method returning Flow<List<T>> work? When does it emit, on which thread does it query, and what are its gotchas?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Room Flow is the most common Flow source in Android apps; interviewers probe invalidation granularity and threading.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The DAO method is cold. On collect, Room runs the query on its query executor (off Main, no need for flowOn), emits the result, then registers an invalidation observer on the tables in the query. Any write to any of those tables, even to rows that are not in my result, triggers a re-query and a new emission. It never completes, so I collect it in a long-lived scope. Gotchas: it re-emits equal lists after unrelated writes, so I add distinctUntilChanged(); and first() is how I get a one-shot read.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Declaration: @Query("SELECT * FROM post ORDER BY ts DESC") fun posts(): Flow<List<Post>>; this is not a suspend function. Room generates the flow using CoroutinesRoom.createFlow (Room 2.x with room-ktx; from Room 2.7 with KMP, the generated code uses the androidx.room.coroutines APIs). Requires room-ktx (Room 2.2+).
  • Invalidation is table-level, not row-level, powered by InvalidationTracker, which uses SQLite triggers writing to a tracking table. Inserting into post re-runs every Flow query that reads post, even WHERE id = 7 queries.
  • Re-query results are emitted each time; Room does not deduplicate. Equal lists are new List objects with equal content, so distinctUntilChanged() (equality on List<Post> which relies on data class equals) filters them.
  • Threading: the query runs on Room's queryExecutor (or the transaction executor if @Transaction); the emission happens in the collector's context, via a channel. No flowOn needed.
  • Cancellation: cancelling the collector unregisters the observer.
  • Collecting is cheap when idle but each collector has its own observer and query. Multiple collectors = multiple queries on each invalidation; use stateIn/shareIn for shared screens.
  • Large result sets are loaded fully into memory per emission; for big lists use Paging.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Dao interface PostDao {
    @Query("SELECT * FROM post ORDER BY ts DESC") fun posts(): Flow<List<Post>>
    @Query("SELECT * FROM post WHERE id = :id") fun post(id: Long): Flow<Post?>
}

val ui = dao.posts().distinctUntilChanged().stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using suspend fun posts(): List<Post> and expecting updates; that is a one-shot read.
  • Calling .single() or .toList() on it; they never complete.
  • Updating a row with identical values: SQLite still fires the trigger, so Room re-emits an identical list.
  • Doing heavy mapping inside map on Main; the emission arrives on the collector's dispatcher.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does a write to an unrelated row cause an emission? → Table-level invalidation.
  2. How do you reduce re-queries on a hot table? → Narrow the query to a smaller table/view, distinctUntilChanged, debounce, or Paging.
  3. Flow vs LiveData from Room? → Same invalidation; Flow is cold and needs your own lifecycle handling (repeatOnLifecycle).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior brings up table-level invalidation, no dedupe, per-collector query cost, and the first() one-shot idiom.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat list re-rendered on every typing-indicator write because indicators lived in the same table; moving them to a separate table cut list emissions by ~95%.

questions.promptHtml: How do you read from Jetpack DataStore with Flow? What does the data flow guarantee, and how should you handle errors?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: DataStore replaced SharedPreferences; its Flow read semantics and error handling are a common check.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: DataStore exposes val data: Flow<Preferences> (or Flow<T> for Proto/typed). It is cold, emits the current persisted value upon collection, then emits again after each successful write, and does not terminate. Reads can throw IOException, so I add .catch { if (it is IOException) emit(emptyPreferences()) else throw it }. For a one-time read I use data.first(). Writes go through edit {} or updateData, which are suspend and transactional.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• First emission happens after the file is read (disk I/O on Dispatchers.IO internally, DataStore's own scope), so collecting from Main is safe.
  • DataStore keeps a single in-memory state per file (one DataStore instance per file is required; creating two instances for the same file throws "There are multiple DataStores active for the same file"). The data flow is derived from it.
  • Updates are serialized and atomic. edit with an unchanged value does not cause a new meaningful emission for equal data (it does not re-emit equal data); still, I add distinctUntilChanged() on mapped fields because mapping Preferences to a field often produces equal values on unrelated key writes.
  • Error behavior: IO errors on read are propagated to the collector as an exception from the flow; CorruptionException is handled via ReplaceFileCorruptionHandler configured on creation.
  • Map to domain: data.map { it[THEME_KEY] ?: "system" }.distinctUntilChanged().

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val Context.store by preferencesDataStore("settings")
private val THEME = stringPreferencesKey("theme")

val theme: Flow<String> = context.store.data
    .catch { if (it is IOException) emit(emptyPreferences()) else throw it }
    .map { it[THEME] ?: "system" }
    .distinctUntilChanged()

suspend fun setTheme(v: String) = context.store.edit { it[THEME] = v }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• runBlocking { store.data.first() } on Main during startup: potential ANR (Q509).
  • Creating the DataStore delegate more than once (inside a class instead of top-level).
  • Catching Exception in .catch and swallowing cancellation or programmer errors.
  • Treating DataStore as a database: it reads the whole file for each change.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not SharedPreferences? → Synchronous reads on Main, apply() ANR on Activity.onStop flush, no error signaling, no transactional update.
  2. Is DataStore data flow hot or cold? → Cold collector API over shared state; each collect gets the current value first.
  3. How do you migrate from SharedPreferences? → SharedPreferencesMigration passed to produceMigrations; runs once before first read.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions the error handling pattern, single-instance requirement, distinctUntilChanged on projections, and the startup read problem.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feature flag read via first() on the cold start path added 120 ms (p90) before first frame on low-end devices; moved to an async preload with a safe default.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app has 1.2M DAU. After a release, the backend team reports /v2/home traffic is up 3.4x with no DAU increase, and p95 backend latency rose from 180 ms to 640 ms. App-side, the Home screen shows three widgets (Hero, Trending, Stats) each in its own Composable/ViewModel collecting repo.homeData(). The code:

class HomeRepo(private val api: HomeApi) {
    fun homeData(): Flow<HomeData> = flow {
        emit(api.getHome())       // network call
    }
}
// Hero VM
val hero = repo.homeData().map { it.hero }.stateIn(viewModelScope, Eagerly, null)
// Trending VM
val trending = repo.homeData().map { it.trending }.stateIn(viewModelScope, Eagerly, null)
// Stats VM
val stats = repo.homeData().map { it.stats }.stateIn(viewModelScope, Eagerly, null)

Charles Proxy shows 3 identical GETs per Home open. Another 0.4x comes from pull-to-refresh, which re-collects. Crash rate and ANR rate are unchanged. A red herring: the CDN cache hit ratio also dropped, which the infra team suspects as the cause.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the traffic 3.4x, and how do you fix it without regressing the architecture?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add caching on the backend" or "add an OkHttp cache". It treats the symptom; the duplication remains, and HTTP cache headers may not even apply to this endpoint.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do all three VMs live in one screen/graph scope? Is the endpoint cacheable (Cache-Control)? When did traffic jump, and which release introduced the split into three widgets? Is pull-to-refresh meant to refetch, or to reuse? Any retry interceptors that might multiply calls?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a client hotfix that collapses to one call, or server-side rate-limit per device for /v2/home (e.g., coalesce within 2 s) while the fix rolls out. Both are low-risk.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) cold Flow re-executes per collector: 3 collectors = 3 calls (matches 3 identical requests per open). (b) Retry interceptor doubling calls: would show duplicates with timing gaps, not simultaneous triplets. (c) CDN changes: the hit ratio drops because requests now arrive in bursts before the first response is cached, a consequence not a cause.
  4. How I'd verify each: Proxy/OkHttp logging interceptor with a request id count per screen open; a unit test with a fake HomeApi counting calls when three collectors collect; compare request timestamps (identical to the millisecond means parallel collectors).
  5. Root cause: flow {} is cold. homeData() is a recipe; each stateIn launches its own collection in its own ViewModel scope, each running api.getHome(). 3 widgets * 1 call = 3x; refreshes add 0.4x, giving the observed ~3.4x.
  6. Fix: Short term: one shared source.
class HomeRepo(private val api: HomeApi, appScope: CoroutineScope) {
    private val refresh = MutableSharedFlow<Unit>(replay = 1).apply { tryEmit(Unit) }
    val home: SharedFlow<HomeData> = refresh
        .mapLatest { api.getHome() }
        .shareIn(appScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), replay = 1)
    fun refresh() { refresh.tryEmit(Unit) }
}
// widgets: repo.home.map { it.hero }

Long term: a single HomeViewModel owning a UiState with the three sections, or a shared parent-scoped ViewModel; the repository owns refresh policy and a short in-memory cache. 7. Prevention: a repository test asserting the API is called once with N collectors (fake API with a counter); a review checklist item "network in flow {} exposed to multiple collectors needs shareIn/stateIn"; a dashboard alert on requests per DAU for top endpoints. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use SharingStarted.Eagerly in an app-scoped repo (calls even when no screen is shown). I would not rely on an HTTP cache to hide the duplication; concurrent identical requests miss the cache anyway. WhileSubscribed(5000) means rotation does not refetch but leaving the screen for >5 s does; that's the intended policy.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the three widgets must show data even when the others fail? → Keep one call, expose Result/sealed state per section; failure in transformation of one section is isolated in map + catch per section.
  • What about the first collector racing the second, with replay = 1? → A late collector gets the replayed value; a collector that arrives while the request is in flight just waits and shares the result.
  • What if appScope outlives logout? → Cancel or reset (resetReplayCache) on logout to avoid stale user data; better scope it to the session component.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a team whose "modular widgets" refactor tripled load on one endpoint; load tests had one collector per scenario, so nobody saw it. They added a "calls per screen open" assertion in the instrumentation suite.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames backend/CDN or adds caching headers.
  • Hire: identifies cold re-execution and uses shareIn/stateIn.
  • Strong hire: also explains WhileSubscribed timeouts, refresh design, scoping/logout, and a test that locks in call counts.

questions.promptHtml: How does cancellation work for a Flow? Is a flow {} with a tight loop cancellable? What does cancellable() do and when do you need it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cancellation is cooperative; interviewers check you know which flows check for it and which do not.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Flow cancellation is the normal coroutine cancellation: cancelling the collector's job cancels the producer, since it runs inside collect. The cooperative check happens at suspension points and, for flow {}, in every emit (via SafeCollector). A flow {} that emits is cancellable; a loop that does CPU work without suspending or emitting is not. Flows built by asFlow() and flowOf historically did not check cancellation on each element; for these (and .asFlow() on ranges/sequences) I add .cancellable() or ensureActive() if the downstream is not suspending.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• flow { emit(x) }: emit checks ensureActive(); cancellation throws CancellationException out of emit and unwinds the producer; finally blocks run.
  • (1..1_000_000).asFlow().collect { heavyCpu(it) } where the collector never suspends: the official Flow guide says flow builders such as asFlow() and flowOf do not perform additional cancellation checks per element (only flow {} via SafeCollector does in the guide's description), so cancellation may not stop the loop promptly. I am not certain how this differs across 1.x versions, so the version-proof rule is: add .cancellable() when a non-suspending collector processes a large asFlow().
  • cancellable() simply inserts an ensureActive() per emission.
  • Operators backed by channels (buffer, flowOn, debounce) are cancellable through channel suspension.
  • first() and take(n) cancel upstream via an internal AbortFlowException; do not catch generic Throwable/Exception in a producer in a way that swallows it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val job = launch {
    (1..Int.MAX_VALUE).asFlow()
        .cancellable()                     // makes cancel effective
        .collect { crunch(it) }            // crunch is non-suspending
}
delay(50); job.cancelAndJoin()

flow {
    try { while (true) { emit(read()); delay(1000) } }
    finally { closeSensor() }              // runs on cancel
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• catch (e: Exception) inside the producer swallowing CancellationException.
  • Assuming the Flow stops immediately: only at the next check/suspension.
  • Doing blocking IO in flow {} (e.g., InputStream.read): not interruptible by cancellation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does finally in the producer run on cancel? → In the producer's coroutine as it unwinds; use withContext(NonCancellable) for suspending cleanup.
  2. Does catch operator catch cancellation? → Not for the collector's own cancellation; it won't turn it into a fallback emission.
  3. How do you test cancellation? → runTest, launch collect, advanceTimeBy, cancel, assert the finally flag.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior knows emit is the check, knows when cancellable() is needed, and treats cleanup in finally with NonCancellable when suspension is needed.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A CSV import via lines.asFlow().map{} kept chewing CPU for 20 s after the user left the screen until .cancellable() was added.

questions.promptHtml: A Flow producer emits every 100 ms and the collector takes 300 ms per item. How long do 3 items take, and why? How does back-pressure work in a plain cold Flow, and what changes with buffer()?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the mental model that a plain Flow is a single coroutine with no queue, and that you can do timing math.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Without a buffer the producer and collector share one coroutine, so emit does not return until the collector finishes that item. Total time is the sum of everything: 3 x (100 + 300) = 1200 ms. Back-pressure is automatic because the producer is suspended inside emit. With buffer() the producer runs in a separate coroutine and puts items in a channel, so the stages overlap: about 100 + 3 x 300 = 1000 ms.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Plain pipeline timeline (producer P = 100 ms, collector C = 300 ms):

P1 [0-100] C1 [100-400] P2 [400-500] C2 [500-800] P3 [800-900] C3 [900-1200]   total 1200 ms

With buffer():

P: P1[0-100] P2[100-200] P3[200-300] (waiting only if buffer full; capacity 64 default)
C:           C1[100-400]  C2[400-700]  C3[700-1000]                           total 1000 ms

Math: the collector is the bottleneck, so total = first production time (100) + 3 x collector time (300) = 1000 ms. Other options:

  • conflate(): buffer of size 1 that overwrites; the collector skips intermediate values. With P=100 and C=300 it sees items 1, 3 (roughly) and finishes sooner. Use for UI state where only the latest matters.
  • collectLatest { }: cancels the collector block when a new value arrives and restarts it.
  • buffer(capacity, onBufferOverflow): SUSPEND (default), DROP_OLDEST, DROP_LATEST. Under the hood buffer, conflate and flowOn fuse into a single channel when adjacent. Details of these operators belong to the buffering chunk; the point here is the default behaviour.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val t = measureTimeMillis {
    flow { repeat(3) { delay(100); emit(it) } }
        .collect { delay(300) }
}                                   // ~1200 ms

val t2 = measureTimeMillis {
    flow { repeat(3) { delay(100); emit(it) } }
        .buffer()
        .collect { delay(300) }
}                                   // ~1000 ms

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming Flow is concurrent by default.
  • Using buffer() and ignoring unbounded memory growth when producer is faster (capacity bounded at 64 by default; Channel.UNLIMITED is unbounded).
  • Expecting conflate() to preserve all values.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where is the back-pressure signal? → The suspension of emit.
  2. Compare with RxJava's Flowable request(n). → Coroutines use suspension instead of demand counting.
  3. How would you make a sensor flow not stall the sensor? → The sensor callback should use callbackFlow with a bounded buffer and an overflow policy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior does the timeline math and states which operator introduces concurrency and why.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A search index flow doing 40 ms of work per item on the collector made the whole downstream producer (a socket reader) fall behind; buffer() with DROP_OLDEST and metrics fixed the lag.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't you call emit from a different coroutine inside flow { } (for example launch { emit(x) })? What do you use instead for concurrent producers?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A frequent real bug; tests understanding of the sequential contract and channelFlow.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: emit isn't thread-safe and must be called from the same coroutine that runs the collector. Calling it from a child launch, even with the same dispatcher, throws "Flow invariant is violated" because the emitting coroutine's Job differs from the collector's. For concurrent producers I use channelFlow { launch { send(x) } }, which is built on a channel, or callbackFlow for callbacks, or combine multiple flows with merge.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The SafeCollector check compares the emission context with the collection context, including the Job. A launch creates a child coroutine with a different Job, thus a different context. The contract serves two purposes: operators like map and onEach can assume sequential invocation (no data races in operator state), and exceptions from downstream have a single path back to the producer.

channelFlow { } gives a ProducerScope, so I can launch children and call send (thread-safe, suspending). The flow collects from the channel in the collector's context, so the contract is preserved at the boundary. callbackFlow is a channelFlow that requires awaitClose.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken
flow {
    coroutineScope { launch { emit(api.a()) }; launch { emit(api.b()) } }   // ISE
}

// Correct
channelFlow {
    launch { send(api.a()) }
    launch { send(api.b()) }
}
// or
merge(flow { emit(api.a()) }, flow { emit(api.b()) })

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using channelFlow when flow {} suffices: extra channel and buffer overhead.
  • Forgetting awaitClose in callbackFlow: throws IllegalStateException at the end of the block.
  • Reaching for withContext + emit to dodge the check.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. send vs trySend? → send suspends if the buffer is full; trySend returns a result immediately, used from non-suspending callbacks.
  2. Does channelFlow change the cold nature? → No, it is still cold; the block runs per collector.
  3. How do you bound concurrency of many launches? → A Semaphore or flatMapMerge(concurrency) over a flow of inputs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior links this to the SafeCollector Job comparison and picks between channelFlow, merge and flatMapMerge by use case.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "parallel loader" using launch { emit } passed unit tests on Unconfined dispatchers and crashed in production under real dispatchers (see Q495).

questions.contextHtml:
A ticketing app shows an order-confirmation number generated locally. Customer support reports ~0.7% of users see different numbers on the confirmation screen and in the e-mail receipt (about 900 tickets/week). Code:

class OrderRepo(private val api: OrderApi) {
    private var counter = 0

    fun placeOrder(cart: Cart): Flow<Receipt> = flow {
        counter++                                   // local sequence for display
        val res = api.submit(cart, clientSeq = counter)
        emit(Receipt(res.id, seq = counter))
    }
}

// ViewModel
val receipt = repo.placeOrder(cart)
fun onConfirm() { viewModelScope.launch { receipt.collect { _ui.value = it } } }
fun onRetryTapped() { viewModelScope.launch { receipt.collect { _ui.value = it } } }

Server logs show two POST /orders for these users 1-3 seconds apart with clientSeq 1 and 2 and the same cart. 100% of affected users tapped Retry after seeing a slow spinner (p95 submit latency is 2.8 s). Red herring: the idempotency key is generated server-side.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and what are the consequences beyond the mismatched number?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make counter volatile/atomic". Misses that the flow re-executes and creates duplicate orders.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are duplicate orders charged? Does the server dedupe? Does the retry button cancel the first collection? How many users hit retry?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the Retry button while a submit is in flight; ask backend for a duplicate-order report and refund/cancel duplicates; support macro for affected users.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the cold flow re-runs the submit on each collect (two POSTs); (b) shared mutable counter in the repository is incremented per run, making the second receipt show seq=2 while the first email shows 1; (c) server race: ruled out by logs.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with a fake API that delays 3 s and two collections; assert the call count; grep server logs for same-cart double POSTs.
  5. Root cause: a flow {} containing a non-idempotent side effect is a recipe; two collect calls = two executions. The counter field is state shared across executions and across users in a singleton repo, so it is also not a per-order value (and not thread-safe).
  6. Fix: A one-shot action is a suspend fun, not a Flow.
suspend fun placeOrder(cart: Cart, idempotencyKey: String): Receipt {
    val res = api.submit(cart, idempotencyKey)
    return Receipt(res.id)
}
// ViewModel
private var submit: Job? = null
fun onConfirm() { if (submit?.isActive == true) return
    val key = pendingKey ?: UUID.randomUUID().toString().also { pendingKey = it }
    submit = viewModelScope.launch {
        _ui.value = try { UiState.Done(repo.placeOrder(cart, key)) }
                    catch (e: IOException) { UiState.Error(e) }   // CancellationException is not caught
    } }

The client-generated idempotency key persists across retries so the server dedupes. 7. Prevention: rule "no non-idempotent work in flow {}", tests asserting one POST under double invocation, idempotency keys on every mutating endpoint. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't shareIn the submit flow to dedupe, since it hides the semantics. I wouldn't use Atomic counters; removing the state is the real fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the user kills the app mid-submit? → Persist pending order with key and resume/reconcile via WorkManager.
  • What if we need progress events? → A Flow of states (Submitting, Done) from the ViewModel, with the actual call in a suspend function.
  • Does stateIn fix it? → It shares executions but ties them to scope lifetime; still unnatural for commands.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: "payment retry" tapped during a 4 s p95 caused 1.1% duplicate holds; the fix was idempotency keys plus single-flight in the ViewModel.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: makes the counter atomic.
  • Hire: identifies re-execution on each collect and switches to suspend fun.
  • Strong hire: adds idempotency keys, in-flight guard, process-death handling and tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A fitness app shows a live workout screen on mid-range devices (3 GB RAM, Android 11). Perfetto shows 11-14 recompositions per second of the entire exercise list (180 items) and Choreographer frame drops: jank rate 18% during workouts. Heart-rate samples (1 write/sec) and rep counts (2 writes/sec) are inserted into workout_event and the UI observes:

@Query("SELECT * FROM exercise WHERE workoutId = :id ORDER BY pos")
fun exercises(id: Long): Flow<List<ExerciseWithSets>>   // @Relation to set, and to workout_event for latest HR

A red herring: someone suspects Compose stability of ExerciseWithSets. Logging shows the DAO flow emits ~3 times per second even though the visible list content changes only when a set is completed (about once per 40 s).
questions.promptHtml: Explain why it emits 3/sec and how you'd cut recomposition and DB load.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add remember / mark class @Stable". Treats Compose, ignores the upstream firehose.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the list really need HR in each item? Which tables does the @Transaction touch? What does ExerciseWithSets include?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add .distinctUntilChanged() after mapping to a UI model that excludes HR; ship quickly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Room's table-level invalidation: any write to workout_event, which the query's @Relation reads, re-runs the whole query and re-emits (3 writes/sec = 3 emissions/sec); (b) Compose instability: possible but secondary; (c) too-large result per emission.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log emission counts in onEach; Room query logging (setQueryCallback) to see re-runs; Perfetto/Layout Inspector recomposition counts; compare list equals between consecutive emissions.
  5. Root cause: Room invalidates by table. The list query joins/relations to workout_event, so every sample causes a re-query of 180 items with relations (~ N+1 sub-queries) and emits a new List instance. Without dedupe, the UI gets a new list 3x/sec; equal content but new references leads to diffing and recomposition.
  6. Fix: Short: .map { it.toUi() }.distinctUntilChanged(). Long: split queries: exercises() reads only exercise/set tables; latestHeartRate(id) reads a one-row query on workout_event and feeds only the HR widget; combine at the ViewModel level with combine if needed; use stable immutable UI models and key in LazyColumn.
  7. Prevention: a debug counter for DAO emissions per second; review rule "Flow queries must only reference tables whose changes matter to that UI"; benchmark with Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't debounce the whole list (adds latency to set completion). I wouldn't throttle writes (loses data). Splitting queries adds more flows to coordinate but isolates churn.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the HR must be shown in each row? → Hold HR in a separate StateFlow<Int> read in the row composable, not in the list item.
  • Does distinctUntilChanged cost anything? → One equals on a 180-item list per emission; far cheaper than recomposition.
  • Would Paging help? → Not for 180 items; helps when rows are thousands.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite where telemetry rows lived in the same table as UI-visible entities; moving telemetry to its own table cut main-thread work by 60%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: focuses on Compose annotations only.
  • Hire: identifies table-level invalidation and adds distinctUntilChanged.
  • Strong hire: splits queries by invalidation domain, verifies with metrics, quantifies the improvement.

questions.contextHtml: You are the tech lead for an app with 6 teams. A shared UserRepository currently exposes suspend fun getUser(id): User, suspend fun getFollowers(id): List<User> and fun observeUser(id): Flow<User> backed by Room. A new engineer proposes making all methods return Flow "for consistency and future live updates", including updateProfile() which would return Flow<Unit>. Another proposes Flow<Result<T>> everywhere. Crash analytics show the main existing pain: 3% of crashes are CancellationException mishandled in runCatching, and unit tests are flaky around first() on Room flows.
questions.promptHtml: Decide the API shape, justify it, and describe the migration plan.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Flow is the modern way, convert everything" or "keep it all as is". No reasoning about semantics.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screens need live updates? How big are follower lists? Who owns error handling (UI or domain)? Are there Java/Views consumers? Are mutating calls retried?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident, so step 2 is a guard: freeze the proposal, fix the 3% crash class (runCatching swallowing cancellation) with a shared suspendRunCatching helper that rethrows CancellationException.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (what could go wrong with all-Flow) (a) one-shot calls become cold flows that re-execute per collector (Q500); (b) mutating Flow<Unit> runs only if collected: forgotten collect = silent no-op; (c) callers must use first() and handle empty/hang; (d) Result flows make cancellation handling worse.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype in one module; count call sites that use .first(); write a test showing an uncollected updateProfile() does nothing.
  5. Root cause: treating "consistency of type" as a goal instead of matching the type to the semantics: one value = suspend; values over time = Flow.
  6. Fix / decision:
interface UserRepository {
    suspend fun getUser(id: Long): User                 // one-shot, main-safe
    suspend fun updateProfile(p: Profile)               // command: suspend, throws on failure
    fun observeUser(id: Long): Flow<User>               // changes over time, backed by Room
    fun followers(id: Long): Flow<PagingData<User>>     // large list: paging, not List
}

Errors: throw domain exceptions from suspend functions; map to UI state at the ViewModel; for streams use catch at the boundary, not Flow<Result>. Migration: add the new APIs alongside, deprecate, migrate team by team with a compat helper; no big bang. 7. Prevention: an API guideline doc: "suspend for one-shot and commands, Flow for observation, Paging for unbounded lists"; a lint/detekt rule for runCatching around suspend calls. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't return Flow from commands. I'd accept the inconsistency between getUser and observeUser as honest, because they have different semantics. I'd not use Flow<Result<T>> since errors in a Flow already have a channel (exception) with defined semantics.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A team wants "get once then keep updated". → observeUser(id) emits current value first (Room does); provide .first() helper for one-shot.
  • Testing? → suspend functions test trivially with runTest; flows via toList with cancellation or Turbine.
  • Java consumers? → Provide callback/CompletableFuture adapters at the boundary.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite where an "all Flow" repository led to a settings save that never ran because the flow wasn't collected on one path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks all-Flow or no-change without reasoning.
  • Hire: matches semantics (suspend vs Flow), explains cold re-execution risk.
  • Strong hire: addresses errors, cancellation, Paging, migration plan, and API guideline enforcement.

questions.promptHtml: How do you unit test a cold Flow? What goes wrong with first(), toList() and runTest virtual time, and when do you use Turbine?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cold flows are easy to test but infinite/hot sources hang tests, and virtual time confuses people.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For a finite cold flow I call toList() inside runTest and assert the list; delays are skipped because runTest uses virtual time. For never-ending flows (Room, DataStore, StateFlow) toList() hangs, so I use take(n).toList(), first(), or Turbine's test {} with awaitItem() and cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents(). I inject dispatchers so flowOn uses the test scheduler, and I check call counts to prove cold re-execution behavior.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• runTest creates a TestScope with a StandardTestDispatcher; delay advances virtual time automatically when everything is idle, so delay(1000) takes ~0 ms real time.
  • flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) in code under test escapes the test scheduler: real threads, real time, and runTest times out after 60 s by default in recent versions (kotlinx-coroutines-test 1.7+: 60 s default, configurable). Inject a CoroutineDispatcher and pass UnconfinedTestDispatcher/StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler).
  • Turbine (app.cash.turbine) collects into a channel; awaitItem(), awaitComplete(), awaitError(), expectNoEvents(); fails if unconsumed events remain at the end of test {} unless cancelled explicitly.
  • Testing cold semantics: count the invocations of the fake source across two collections.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Test fun emitsInOrder() = runTest {
    val f = flow { emit(1); delay(1_000); emit(2) }
    assertEquals(listOf(1, 2), f.toList())
}

@Test fun roomLike() = runTest {
    repo.observe().test {                 // Turbine
        assertEquals(Loading, awaitItem())
        fakeDao.insert(x)
        assertEquals(Loaded(listOf(x)), awaitItem())
        cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
    }
}

@Test fun coldRunsTwice() = runTest {
    var calls = 0
    val f = flow { calls++; emit(1) }
    f.first(); f.first()
    assertEquals(2, calls)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• toList() on a StateFlow/Room fake: hangs until the test timeout.
  • Hard-coded Dispatchers.IO in repositories.
  • Using Dispatchers.setMain incorrectly, so the collector runs on a different scheduler from the test scheduler.
  • Asserting using real time (delay + System.currentTimeMillis).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to test a flowOn pipeline? → Inject the dispatcher and use the test dispatcher.
  2. How to assert "no extra emissions"? → Turbine's expectNoEvents() after advanceUntilIdle().
  3. How to test a cancelled collector runs finally? → Launch collect in backgroundScope/a job, cancel, assert flag.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior brings up virtual time, dispatcher injection, Turbine's strictness, and tests for cold-ness and cancellation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flaky CI test (1 in 30 failures) used Dispatchers.IO in the repo; making the dispatcher injectable removed the flakiness.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app (3.5M MAU, 70% of sessions on Android 9-12) has 140 RxJava 2 call sites in the data layer: Observable<T> for streams, Single<T> for requests, Completable for commands. You are asked to migrate to coroutines/Flow module by module, shipping weekly, with no regression in crash-free rate (currently 99.62%). In a pilot module the first migrated code looked like:

fun prices(): Flow<Price> = priceSocket.observe().asFlow()   // Observable -> Flow via rxjava2 interop
val disposable = prices().subscribe(...)                      // does not exist: someone tried to port subscribe()

Pilot results: 2 crashes in beta, UndeliverableException disappeared, but a new 0.3% of sessions show a stuck loading spinner. A red herring: someone blames the interop library version.
questions.promptHtml: How do you plan the migration and what semantic differences between Observable and cold Flow do you watch for?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace Observable with Flow and Single with Flow." Ignores semantic gaps: error handling, threading, completion, hot vs cold, and subscription lifecycle.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which Rx subjects (BehaviorSubject, PublishSubject) are hot and shared? Which streams are infinite? Who consumes (ViewModels, Java classes)? Test coverage? Are there observeOn/subscribeOn chains encoding threading?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause rollout of the pilot module at 5%/20% staged rollout; revert the spinner bug via a server-driven flag if the module is flagged. Staged rollouts allow a halt at the first spike.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) a Single mapped to Flow that never completes or is collected after completion differently; (b) BehaviorSubject (hot with replay) replaced by a cold flow; late collectors lose the current value or re-fire the request; (c) error semantics: Rx onError terminates the stream; in Flow an uncaught exception cancels the collecting scope (viewModelScope child) leaving the spinner un-hidden; (d) interop version: red herring unless evidence.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare Crashlytics non-fatals and loading-state logs; characterization tests for each migrated stream (record Rx behaviour: values, completion, error); add a debug assertion for "loading state exited".
  5. Root cause (typical): In the pilot, an error in the network stream escaped as an exception inside launchIn, cancelling the collector, so hideLoading() in doOnComplete equivalent never ran. Rx had .doFinally { hideLoading() }; the port omitted onCompletion.
  6. Fix / plan: Mapping table:
Rx Coroutines
Single<T>, Maybe<T> suspend fun(): T / T?
Completable suspend fun()
cold Observable<T> Flow<T>
BehaviorSubject MutableStateFlow
PublishSubject MutableSharedFlow
observeOn/subscribeOn collector context / flowOn
doFinally onCompletion / try-finally
onErrorReturn catch { emit(..) }
CompositeDisposable scope / Job
Do it bottom-up: leaf data sources first with kotlinx-coroutines-rx2 adapters (asFlow, .await(), rxSingle {}, rxObservable {}) at the seams so callers don't change; then flip callers; then delete adapters. One module per release, behind staged rollout and a kill switch.
  1. Prevention: characterization tests, a migration checklist (completion, errors, threading, hot/cold, replay), Crashlytics keys for migrated modules.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't big-bang. I wouldn't convert subjects blindly to SharedFlow without choosing replay. I'd accept adapters for several weeks; they cost a thread hop per element but reduce risk.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What about Observable.error leaking UndeliverableException? → Gone with Flow since errors propagate through structured concurrency, but check RxJavaPlugins.setErrorHandler until Rx is removed.
  • Backpressure in Flowable? → Replaced by suspension; if the old code used onBackpressureDrop, use buffer(DROP_LATEST)/conflate.
  • Thread-safety of BehaviorSubject.onNext from many threads? → MutableStateFlow.update {} is thread-safe.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite migration where Single.cache() semantic (memoized result) was lost; the request ran for every observer until replaced by async in a shared scope or shareIn.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: mechanical 1:1 replacement.
  • Hire: maps types by semantics and plans incremental migration with adapters.
  • Strong hire: identifies error, completion, hot/cold, threading differences and a verification strategy with staged rollout.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review for a release that raised the ANR rate from 0.35% to 1.4% (Play Console threshold is 0.47% user-perceived ANR; you are in the bad-behavior zone). Affected: 60% on devices with 2-3 GB RAM and eMMC storage, concentrated at cold start. Trace from Play Console:

"main" prio=5 tid=1 Waiting
  at java.lang.Object.wait
  at kotlinx.coroutines.BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking(Builders.kt:...)
  at kotlinx.coroutines.BuildersKt__BuildersKt.runBlocking(Builders.kt:...)
  at com.app.Prefs.getToken(Prefs.kt:22)
  at com.app.AuthInterceptor.intercept(AuthInterceptor.kt:14)   // runs on OkHttp thread
  ...
  at com.app.App.onCreate(App.kt:41)

The commit: "Migrate SharedPreferences to DataStore". Code:

fun getToken(): String = runBlocking { ctx.store.data.map { it[TOKEN] ?: "" }.first() }

Also App.onCreate calls Prefs.getFlagsBlocking() the same way. A red herring: Firebase init time grew by 30 ms in the same release.
questions.promptHtml: What happened, what's the root cause, and what changes prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "DataStore is slow, go back to SharedPreferences." Or "wrap with Dispatchers.IO" without explaining that blocking Main is the problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which threads call getToken (trace shows Main at App.onCreate and OkHttp threads)? Size of the DataStore file? First read or every read? Any migration (SharedPreferencesMigration) on first launch?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix with staged rollout halt; make App.onCreate not block: read flags async with defaults; cache the token in memory after first read.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) runBlocking on Main in onCreate waits for the first DataStore read plus one-time SharedPreferences migration on slow eMMC; (b) OkHttp interceptor blocking pool threads on each request; (c) Firebase init: 30 ms, below ANR impact; (d) DataStore deadlock: if the DataStore scope uses a dispatcher that the blocked thread is needed for.
  4. How I'd verify each: Play Console ANR clusters and stack traces; Perfetto cold-start trace with Trace.beginSection; StrictMode detectDiskReads in dev; measure first data.first() duration (migration) on a low-end device.
  5. Root cause: SharedPreferences was effectively already loaded in memory after first access; DataStore must read and deserialize the file (and run migration) asynchronously, and the first call can take 100-800 ms on slow storage. runBlocking on Main converts that latency directly into frozen UI. data never completes, so first() is what ends it, but the wait is still blocking.
  6. Fix: Short: non-blocking startup: App.onCreate launches appScope.launch { flags = store.data.first() } with safe defaults. Interceptor reads from an in-memory @Volatile token cache populated by collecting store.data in an app scope at startup; if not yet loaded, wait with timeout in the interceptor thread (never Main). Long: an AuthTokenProvider that exposes StateFlow<String?> and a suspend awaitToken(); use Authenticator/suspend-friendly OkHttp wrappers.
class TokenCache(store: DataStore<Preferences>, scope: CoroutineScope) {
    val token: StateFlow<String?> = store.data.map { it[TOKEN] }
        .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, null)
}
  1. Prevention: StrictMode in debug, a lint/detekt rule banning runBlocking in app code, startup benchmark (Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric) in CI with a regression threshold, ANR dashboards per release.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't revert to SharedPreferences (it can block Main on apply()/commit() flush too).
