I wouldn't paper over with Dispatchers.IO inside runBlocking; the caller still blocks. The cost of the in-memory cache is a small risk of stale reads, acceptable with a collector.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the token is needed for the very first request? → Use AppStartup/splash gating on awaitToken() in a coroutine, not a blocking call.
  • Could first() deadlock? → If the DataStore's own scope/dispatcher is blocked by the caller, yes; do not block IO threads that the store needs.
  • Why did QA not see it? → Fast flash storage and warm caches on test devices; add a low-end device to the matrix.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite where a "mechanical" migration PR touched 40 call sites and kept runBlocking; the cold-start p90 rose 400 ms on low-end devices.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: reverts or switches dispatchers inside runBlocking.
  • Hire: removes blocking on Main, caches in memory, adds safe defaults.
  • Strong hire: explains the migration/first-read latency, adds guards (StrictMode, benchmarks, lint), and handles the first-request token problem.

questions.promptHtml: Which Flow sources complete and which never do? How does that affect toList(), single(), code after collect, and onCompletion?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many hangs come from assuming a stream terminates.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A flow completes when its producer block returns. flow { } with a finite body, flowOf, asFlow(), and a single network call wrapped in flow {} complete. Room queries, DataStore data, StateFlow, SharedFlow and callbackFlow with awaitClose do not complete on their own; they end only when the collector is cancelled or an operator like first()/take(n) cancels upstream. Terminal operators that need completion (toList, single, count, fold, reduce) hang on those, and code after collect {} never runs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Source Completes? Safe terminal ops
flowOf, asFlow, finite flow{} yes all
flow { emit(api.get()) } yes all
Room Flow<T> no first(), take(n), collect in a scope
DataStore data no first(), collect
StateFlow/SharedFlow never first(), collect
callbackFlow when close() or producer ends depends
flow { while (true) ... } no first(), take

onCompletion { cause -> } runs when the flow completes normally (cause null), fails (cause is the exception), or is cancelled (cause is CancellationException). It is a "finally" for the stream and sees upstream exceptions without catching them (they continue downstream). It is not invoked at some arbitrary time for hot flows, since they don't complete; use it in the collecting coroutine's finally.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
viewModelScope.launch {
    _loading.value = true
    repo.items().collect { render(it) }   // Room: never returns
    _loading.value = false                // never runs
}
// Better
repo.items().onStart { _loading.value = true }.onEach { _loading.value = false; render(it) }.launchIn(viewModelScope)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• dao.items().toList() or .single(): hangs.
  • Using onCompletion to hide a spinner for a hot flow.
  • first() on a flow that may be empty and completes: NoSuchElementException.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you turn an endless stream into a finite one? → take(n), takeWhile, first, or a timeout via withTimeout.
  2. Does cancelling the collector invoke onCompletion? → Yes, with a CancellationException cause.
  3. What if the producer throws? → onCompletion runs with the exception, then the exception continues downstream unless a catch handles it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior categorizes sources, knows which terminals are safe, and does UI state transitions with onStart/onEach rather than relying on code after collect.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Many "spinner forever" bugs trace back to hiding the loader after collect on an endless flow (see Q512).

questions.promptHtml: What is the runtime cost of Flow, and when is Flow the wrong tool? Think of 1M elements or 60 events per second.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests judgment: Flow is great for async streams but not free for CPU-bound bulk transformations.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A plain operator pipeline costs one lambda call per operator per element plus boxing for primitives; it is cheap per element (tens of nanoseconds) but not zero. Operators that introduce coroutines/channels (flowOn, buffer, flatMapMerge, combine, debounce) add a context switch and channel hand-off per element, which is microseconds. For 1M in-memory numbers, a Sequence or a plain loop is much faster, and for batch processing I process chunks (chunked-style windowing) instead of per-element flows. At UI event rates (60/s) the cost is irrelevant; the problem is what the collector does with each value.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Allocation: each operator creates a Flow object at assembly time (once), and each collect creates collector lambda objects per collection, not per element. Per element, values of Int/Long get boxed because Flow<T> is generic.
  • Suspension: each emit is a suspend call, creating a continuation state machine; non-suspending paths are fast, but resumed delay or dispatch costs ~1-10 microseconds.
  • Channel-backed operators: send/receive with dispatching across threads when flowOn changes dispatcher. For 1M elements through flowOn(Default) the hand-off cost dominates (order of seconds vs tens of milliseconds for a direct loop; measure with Macrobenchmark/JMH, don't trust my numbers).
  • Practical pattern: batch inside the producer (read 500 rows, emit List<Row>), reduce per-element overhead, and emit domain-level units, not bytes.
  • Do not use Flow for high-frequency sensor data to the UI without conflate/sample; UI only needs the latest per frame (16.6 ms).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// 1M elements: per element hand-off
(1..1_000_000).asFlow().flowOn(Dispatchers.Default).map { it * 2 }.collect { }
// Better: process in a plain loop, or batch
(1..1_000_000).chunked(1_000).asFlow().map { chunk -> chunk.sumOf { it * 2L } }.collect { }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Per-row flows (Flow<Row>) from a database for bulk export instead of batches.
  • Chaining flowOn repeatedly "to be safe".
  • Micro-optimizing Flow when the real cost is JSON parsing or layout.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you check the cost? → Macrobenchmark / Perfetto traces, measureNanoTime in a JMH-like loop.
  2. Sequence vs Flow for 1M in-memory items? → Sequence for sync CPU work; Flow if the stages suspend.
  3. How do you cap UI update rate? → sample(16)/conflate plus collecting on Main.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior separates assembly cost from per-element cost, identifies channel operators as the expensive ones, and prescribes batching and measurement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A log uploader using per-line Flow<String> with flowOn consumed 25% CPU on low-end devices; batching 200 lines per emission cut it to under 5%.

questions.contextHtml:
An e-commerce app's Orders screen shows a progress bar forever for 4% of sessions, primarily returning users with cached orders. Support tickets say "orders load, then spinner keeps spinning". No crash, no ANR. After a refactor from LiveData to Flow:

fun load() = viewModelScope.launch {
    _state.value = State.Loading
    orderDao.observeOrders().collect { _state.value = State.Content(it) }
    _state.value = State.Idle        // "hide spinner"
}
fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch {
    _state.value = State.Loading
    val fresh = api.orders()          // may throw IOException
    orderDao.replaceAll(fresh)
    _state.value = State.Idle
}

UI shows spinner when state is Loading || refreshing; a second bar is displayed during Content if refreshing. Logs: refresh threw UnknownHostException in 90% of affected sessions (offline on metro), with no catch. The team also notes first-launch (no cache) users are fine. Red herring: Room version bump.
questions.promptHtml: Explain why the spinner never disappears and fix it. Also note two other defects.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap in try/catch and set Idle" for refresh only, and ignore the dead line after collect.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What drives the spinner exactly? Is refresh() called from init? What does the UI show for Content + offline? How does the old LiveData version represent loading?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-flag/hotfix to hide the spinner when Content arrives; ship a patch release; no data migration needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) collect on a Room flow never returns, so State.Idle is dead code; (b) in refresh, an exception skips Idle and (as it is thrown inside launch in viewModelScope) goes to the thread's uncaught handler: would crash, unless a CoroutineExceptionHandler swallows it; the logs show swallowed UnknownHostException, so state is stuck at Loading; (c) Room bump: red herring.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add logging after collect; unit test with fake DAO flow that never completes and assert the final state; simulate airplane mode with a fake API that throws; check the handler installed on the scope.
  5. Root cause: Two separate state transitions depend on code that never executes: the line after an endless collect, and the line after a throwing network call. First-launch users have no cached emission order differences, so they hit a different path (the API success sets Idle).
  6. Fix: Make state derived, not imperatively toggled.
private val refreshing = MutableStateFlow(false)
private val error = MutableStateFlow<Throwable?>(null)

val ui: StateFlow<UiState> = combine(orderDao.observeOrders(), refreshing, error) { orders, r, e ->
    UiState(orders = orders, refreshing = r, error = e)
}.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), UiState())

fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch {
    refreshing.value = true
    try { orderDao.replaceAll(api.orders()); error.value = null }
    catch (e: IOException) { error.value = e }
    finally { refreshing.value = false }
}

Other defects: swallowing exceptions via a blanket handler hides the failure; load() can be called twice and start two collectors. 7. Prevention: a rule that cleanup/state resets go in finally/onCompletion/derived state, never "after collect"; tests with never-completing fakes and failing APIs; offline scenario in QA. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't add a timeout to hide the spinner; it masks the bug. I wouldn't catch Exception (it would swallow CancellationException) in refresh.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can I use onCompletion for the DB flow? → It won't run until cancellation; wrong tool for a stream that never ends.
  • What about showing cached data with an offline banner? → Derived UiState.error plus Content, which the combine already supports.
  • What about launchIn double-calls? → Keep the collector in init or use stateIn, so only one exists.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from a LiveData-to-Flow migration where "dead code after collect" produced a different stuck state on three screens; found by a lint-like grep for collect { followed by statements.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds try/catch to refresh only.
  • Hire: spots endless collect, moves state into derived flows or onEach/finally.
  • Strong hire: also finds the swallowed-exception handler and double-collector risk, and prescribes tests with never-completing fakes.
